title: Judicial Renaissance -- Ch. 9: Judging the Judges
keywords: New Code of Judicial Conduct for the Philippine Judiciary
the ships that plague public service
knowing everything about something and something about everything
Aim high and hit the mark
primary_topics: Chapter 9 of 'Judicial Renaissance' -- an address to the fifth anniversary of Bantay Katarungan and the monthly forum of Kilosbayan in which CJP proposes four essential attributes, the 'four Ins,' as the standards by which a citizens' watchdog may judge the judges.

Integrity as more than honesty: the capacity, illustrated by martial-law-era heroes and by jurists on the Bantayog Wall of Remembrance, to denounce wrong and promote truth, together with impartiality and the appearance of propriety.

Independence from the 'ships' that plague public service -- kinships, relationships, friendships and fellowship -- and from a misplaced sense of gratitude to the appointing authority, argued through the example of Earl Warren.

Industry and intelligence: the crushing caseloads of the Supreme Court and the trial courts, and the demand that judges know everything about something and something about everything, closing with a plea for judicial compensation, exemption from the Salary Standardization Law and a lump-sum judicial appropriation.
sub_topics: CJP opens on the tradition that justices live in fortress-like isolation as gods of Mt. Olympus, better read than heard, and says he is breaking that tradition in obedience to Senator Jovito R. Salonga's summons.

He describes Salonga as his dean, professor, first boss and role model for over 40 years, and sums up his foremost teaching: aspire more ardently for the things money cannot buy -- excellence, ethics, honor, character and a reverential regard for God.

He situates the talk in the judiciary's ongoing transformation under the APJR begun by Chief Justice Davide, whose target he abbreviates as CID -- corruption, incompetence and delay in the rendition of judgments.

He argues that while computers, research facilities and stately courtrooms can be bought, justice is ultimately delivered by human beings who must be upright, credible and competent -- qualities money cannot buy.

He reconciles the Constitution's four qualities (competence, integrity, probity and independence) with the New Code of Judicial Conduct's seven, encapsulating them as four Ins: integrity, independence, industry and intelligence.
Integrity is defined as going beyond refusal to tell a falsehood to encompass the moral courage to denounce a wrong and promote the truth.

He contrasts martial-law officials who merely kept themselves personally pure with those who actively worked at risk of safety, possessions and careers to restore freedom -- naming Chief Justices Roberto Concepcion and Claudio Teehankee and Justice Calixto Zaldivar as jurists honored on the Bantayog Wall of Remembrance.

Integrity also includes intellectual decency and personal honor transcending acclaim, and impartiality -- duties performed without fear or favor, conduct above reproach, and avoidance of undue social contact with litigants and lawyers.

Asked by a business leader why justices refuse to socialize with experts who might enlighten them, he replied that all argument must be heard in court in the presence of all parties, as demanded by fairness and the appearance of fairness.

He tells the Frivaldo story: Juan Frivaldo's repeated attempts in early 1996 to see him, his own steadfast refusal, Frivaldo's despairing remark to journalist Max Soliven that he would flee to the jungles of Sorsogon, and the decision CJP later penned recognizing his citizenship.

Meeting Frivaldo a year later, CJP told him he owed him nothing, explained that propriety had barred contact, and observed that his victory was sweeter because it was not the result of lakad but of an impartial assessment of law and facts.

Independence requires magistrates to decide only on the rational relationship between law and facts, free of the 'ships' -- kinships, relationships, friendships and fellowship -- that plague public service.
He recounts declining a sizeable retainer a decade earlier when a wealthy businessman asked whether his firm knew the judge as well as the law.

Independence also means freedom from emotional baggage and misplaced gratitude to the appointing authority, illustrated by Earl Warren, greeted with hoots as a mere politician but becoming the government's conscience to Eisenhower's consternation and, per William Douglas, approaching John Marshall in esteem.
Industry demands a personal passion for work extending into evenings and early mornings when judges find solitude to wrestle with their consciences and gather courage.

He quantifies the Supreme Court's load: about 6,000 pending cases, roughly 400 per justice among the 15 incumbents, 25 to 30 new cases raffled monthly, so each must dispose of at least 30 a month by rejection, resolution or ponencia.
He adds his own extra duties as senior justice and Division chairperson, chairperson of the House of Representatives Electoral Tribunal, and chair of several judicial reform committees.

He describes Chief Justice Davide's heavier load -- over 60 percent of his time on administration, days from 5:30 a.m. to 8:30 p.m. -- calling him an even more industrious administrator than decision writer.

Lower-court statistics as of July 31, 2004 show 343,875 cases pending in RTCs and 445,999 in first-level courts, giving averages of about 464 and 695 cases per judge with a third of courts vacant, and some courts carrying as many as 6,000 cases.
Constitutional deadlines of 3, 12 and 24 months for trial, appellate and Supreme Court cases are read as demanding not just speed but industry, since there is just too much work to do.

Intelligence covers knowledge and wisdom -- mastery of law plus familiarity with all branches of knowledge, so that judges are not merely walking databases of the Constitution, the law and jurisprudence.

He lists eight illustrations of that breadth: the 1995 Mining Law ruling, cyanide fishing and coral reefs, the emerging economic paradigms behind the WTO ruling, mathematics in the party-list formula and in interest and sentence computation, DNA testing, battered woman syndrome, Canon Law behind Article 36 psychological incapacity, and accounting knowledge in striking down unilateral interest charges.
He proposes that Bantay Katarungan use the four Ins as standards, assigning percentages and a passing mark, in the spirit of the motto 'Aim high and hit the mark.'

He couples high standards with a duty to compensate properly, citing the 34 percent trial-court vacancy rate despite recent increases, and urges exemption from the Salary Standardization Law and a lump-sum judicial appropriation of about two percent of the national budget with SC discretion to allocate it.
He closes by inviting the group to be ever vigilant sentinels of justice -- mga bantay ng katarungan -- quoting the refrain of 'Impossible Dream.'

stances.claim: Judicial reform ultimately turns on the judge: electronic research facilities, computerized processes and stately courtrooms can be bought, but justice is delivered by human beings who must be upright, credible and competent -- qualities that money cannot buy.
stances.rhetorical_move: money-can-buy versus money-cannot-buy antithesis, borrowed from Salonga's teaching and applied to the reform program itself

stances.claim: Integrity in a judge goes beyond honesty: it requires the moral courage to denounce a wrong and promote the truth, so that merely keeping oneself clean under an authoritarian regime is not enough.
stances.rhetorical_move: graded moral comparison between the merely honest and the actively courageous, anchored in named jurists on the Bantayog Wall of Remembrance

stances.claim: A judge must not only be impartial but also be perceived to be so, which is why all argument must be heard in court in the presence of all parties and why undue social contact with litigants and lawyers must be avoided.
stances.rhetorical_move: appearance-of-fairness principle demonstrated autobiographically through the Frivaldo refusal rather than asserted abstractly

stances.claim: Independence requires freedom from the 'ships' of public service -- kinships, relationships, friendships and fellowship -- and from misplaced gratitude to the appointing authority.
stances.rhetorical_move: coinage plus counterexample: a memorable label for the problem, then Earl Warren as proof that an appointee can become the appointer's conscience

stances.claim: Setting strict and high standards for judging judges creates a concomitant duty to compensate them properly, which requires exempting the judiciary from the Salary Standardization Law and granting a lump-sum appropriation of about two percent of the national budget for the Court to allocate.
stances.rhetorical_move: reciprocity argument turned into a concrete legislative ask, backed by the 34 percent trial-court vacancy rate

notable_anecdotes: CJP explains that he broke the tradition of judicial isolation only because his revered guru Jovito R. Salonga -- his dean, professor and first boss, whom he had regarded with awe for over 40 years -- summoned him to the Bantay Katarungan anniversary.

At an open forum before foreign chambers of commerce, a business leader asked why justices refuse to socialize with experts who might enlighten them on scientific or economic aspects of a case; CJP replied that all discussion must happen in court before all parties.

The Frivaldo episode: newly appointed in early 1996, CJP steadfastly refused Juan Frivaldo's repeated approaches through his secretary and mutual friends, and Frivaldo told journalist Max Soliven he would just flee to the jungles of Sorsogon -- 'Mamumundok na lang ako' -- certain he would lose again.

A few months later CJP penned the decision recognizing Frivaldo's citizenship; meeting him a year afterward, he told the grateful governor he owed him nothing and that his victory was sweeter because it was not the result of lakad.

A decade before, a wealthy businessman told CJP that while his firm had bar topnotchers, 'it is good to know the law, but it is even better to know the judge' -- whereupon he and his partners declined the case despite losing a sizeable retainer.

He recounts Earl Warren being greeted with hoots and groans as a mere politician and bluffer, only to become, to Eisenhower's consternation, the government's conscience and a judicial icon whose esteem William Douglas likened to John Marshall's.
He reports Chief Justice Davide's own admission that he spends more than 60 percent of his time administering the judiciary, beginning each day in his office at 5:30 a.m. and ending at 8:30 p.m.

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 9 of 'Judicial Renaissance' collects an address Justice Panganiban gave at the fifth anniversary of Bantay Katarungan and the monthly forum of Kilosbayan, opening with the tradition that justices live in fortress-like isolation as gods of Mt. Olympus, better read than heard, and explaining that he broke it in obedience to his revered guru Jovito R. Salonga, whose foremost teaching was to aspire more ardently for the things money cannot buy. Noting that the judiciary was being transformed by the Action Program for Judicial Reform against what he abbreviates as CID -- corruption, incompetence and delay -- he argued that computers and courtrooms can be bought but upright, credible and competent judges cannot, and encapsulated the Constitution's and the New Code's lists of judicial qualities into four Ins: integrity, independence, industry and intelligence. Integrity, he said, exceeds honesty and requires the moral courage to denounce wrong, distinguishing martial-law officials who merely kept themselves pure from those who risked everything, among them Chief Justices Concepcion and Teehankee and Justice Zaldivar on the Bantayog Wall of Remembrance; it also demands impartiality and the appearance of propriety, which he illustrated by his refusal to meet Juan Frivaldo in 1996 -- prompting Frivaldo to tell Max Soliven he would flee to the jungles of Sorsogon -- before penning the decision that recognized his citizenship, and by his later explanation to Frivaldo that the victory was sweeter for not being the result of lakad. Independence, the second In, requires freedom from the 'ships' that plague public service -- kinships, relationships, friendships and fellowship -- and from gratitude to the appointing authority, as Earl Warren showed by becoming Eisenhower's conscience. Industry he documented with caseload figures: some 6,000 cases pending in the Supreme Court, about 400 per justice, and 343,875 and 445,999 cases in the RTCs and first-level courts as of July 31, 2004. Intelligence he equated with excellence, knowing everything about something and something about everything, listing eight rulings that demanded mining, marine, economic, mathematical, genetic, psychological, canonical and accounting knowledge. He urged Bantay Katarungan to score judges on the four Ins, and coupled that with a plea for exemption from the Salary Standardization Law and a lump-sum judicial appropriation, closing on the refrain of 'Impossible Dream.'
